title: Gentleness toward others (III.8)
hookLine: a sharp message lands, and this time you're right; Francis de Sales still says don't let the anger in
tomorrow: you mess up, again. how should you talk to yourself?

lines: SHORT, SHARP, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
WHY SHUT THE DOOR ON FAIR ANGER?
cards: A message lands, short and sharp, in front of everyone. And this time you're right: it was unfair. Your thumbs are already typing.
Here's the odd part. Francis de Sales says don't let the anger in. Not the petty kind, not even the fair kind.
Why would anyone shut the door on anger that's justified?

teach.h: LEARN OF ME, FOR I AM MEEK.
teach.b: Start with the pattern Francis builds on, Christ's words in the Douay-Rheims: "Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart." Meekness is the old word for gentleness toward others. Now the puzzle.
Francis leans on Augustine: it's better to refuse anger entry altogether, even anger that seems just, than to let a little in. His reason is how anger behaves.
Once it's inside, it settles, and what came in small grows large. Easier to keep it out than to get it out. So what do you do when it rises anyway?

Gather yourself, he says, but gently, not violently, because fighting anger with fury only stirs it up. And call for help, the way the disciples woke Jesus in the storm: "Lord, save us, we perish." Then the answer itself.
Proverbs puts it plainly: "A mild answer breaketh wrath: but a harsh word stirreth up fury." And if you slip and snap?
Make it right quickly, Francis says, with a gentle word or act toward the very person you were sharp with. This isn't pretending nothing happened. The unfair thing can still be named.
It just gets named by someone who isn't on fire.

how: Catholics count gentleness among the fruits of the Holy Spirit; some examine themselves on anger at night and bring sharp words to confession, and making amends to the person is part of the repair.

o: staying quiet so you never cause anyone trouble
being kind only to the people who are kind to you
answering others' anger calmly, without anger of your own

games.q: gentleness toward others — tap the pairs.
p: learn of me, because I am meek
gather yourself gently, call for help
repair it fast, toward that person

s: meekness means letting people walk all over you
it's strength that chooses not to strike back; the wrong can still be named calmly.
Francis says even anger that seems just is better kept out
once inside, it settles and grows. easier to keep it out than get it out.
if you snap at someone, Francis says to wait for them to apologize first
he says make it right quickly, with a gentle word or act toward that person.

games.q: at a family dinner your uncle mocks your cousin's new job, and he's plainly wrong. your cousin goes red. what would Francis's meekness do first?
o: answer him calmly and briefly, without heat.
match his tone so he knows he's wrong.
stay silent all night and let it go.
games.why: a mild answer breaks wrath. gentleness still answers; it just doesn't answer with fury.

practice: Close your hands into fists, slowly, then open them all the way and leave them resting open on your lap. Through the sit, if a sharp word from this week comes back, keep the hands open and let a gentle reply take shape.

wordCard.voice: Gentleness toward others. Meekness: answering anger without anger, and keeping it from settling in.

orig.note: Greek for meek, gentle: the word in Matthew 11:29, rendered meek in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Keep this one: gentle answer, the kind that breaks wrath and still answers. Until tomorrow.
